vignette:
He is a 42-year-old Pacific Islander man who comes to treatment after an assault that changed the way he moves through the world. Before the attack, he describes himself as steady and practical, someone who works with his hands and takes pride in being the person others call when the wiring fails or a job needs to be finished properly. As an electrician, he is used to ladders, confined spaces, and the normal risks of the trade. He understands danger in a technical way. What he did not expect was how vulnerable he would feel in a place that was supposed to be ordinary.

The assault happens after work, on a routine evening that should have ended like any other. He is heading to his vehicle when a group of men approach him, and the encounter turns violent almost immediately. He recalls being struck, shoved, and surrounded, with only fragments of the event staying clear in his mind: the sound of his own breathing, the glare of lights, the shock of realizing he is not able to reason his way out of it. He reports that time seems to slow and speed up at once. He does not fight back the way he imagines he should have. Instead, he freezes, then scrambles to protect himself, feeling humiliated by how powerless he is. Even now, he describes that moment as something more than fear; it is a complete loss of control.

In the days afterward, he is physically injured and emotionally disoriented. He tries to return to work too quickly, telling himself that staying busy will keep him from thinking about it. At first he manages short jobs, but even simple tasks become difficult because his attention keeps drifting to the possibility that someone is behind him or watching him. He begins checking exits, scanning parking lots, and choosing routes that let him see approaching traffic. He no longer likes being the first one on a site or the last one to leave. He notices that he is tense in his shoulders and jaw most of the day, as if his body has not gotten the message that the assault is over.

At home, his partner sees that he is different. He is quieter and more easily irritated. Small things set him off: a car door slamming outside, someone raising their voice on television, a sudden touch from behind. He startles hard and then feels ashamed for reacting so strongly. He sleeps lightly and wakes often, sometimes from dreams that leave him sweating and unable to settle back down. On some nights he avoids sleep as long as possible because he does not want to face what will happen when he closes his eyes. When the memories come, they are not like a full story but flashes that arrive without permission — the impact of a blow, the sound of footsteps, the feeling of being trapped. He says the memories do not stay in the past; they come back with the same force as if they are happening again.

He also notices himself pulling away from people. He still goes to work and keeps up appearances, but he feels detached, as if part of him is standing at a distance watching the rest of him get through the day. He stops going to gatherings where there might be unfamiliar men, and he avoids the street where the assault occurred. Even errands become complicated because he plans them around how crowded the parking lot will be and whether he can get in and out quickly. He does not like admitting how much his world has shrunk. As a man who has always been relied upon, he finds it especially difficult to sit with the fact that he now feels afraid in places that used to be ordinary.

Over time, his sense of safety does not return on its own. He becomes preoccupied with what he might have done differently, replaying the event and wondering whether he should have seen it coming or moved faster. The self-questioning mixes with anger, and he feels resentment toward the men who attacked him, toward the bystanders who did not help, and toward his own body for failing to protect him. Despite this, he is careful not to let his anger show too much. He says he was raised to keep going, to not make a burden of himself, and he still tries to hold that line. Yet the strain is visible in the way he carries himself: guarded, watchful, and tired in a way that rest does not seem to touch.

By the time he begins to speak openly about the assault, he has already been living with its effects for months. He remains in a relationship and continues working, but both require more effort than before. He wants to return to being the version of himself who felt capable and unafraid, but he is still learning how deeply the attack has altered his trust in his surroundings and in his own body.
